---
title: "Conventions across tools"
description: >
  Why igraph, NetworkX, sna, and UCINET give different numbers for the same
  measure, and how the convention argument reproduces each.
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

"Closeness centrality" names a family of formulas, not one number.
Programs differ in how they count ties, normalize scores, and treat nodes
that cannot reach each other, and their documentation rarely puts those
choices side by side. A published result should say which was used, and
replicating a study done in another program should take one argument, not
a reimplementation.

knappnet records every such difference in one place (in the engine's
source, `conventions.rs`, and in `?conventions`) and exposes it as an
argument:

```r
measure(g, convention = "igraph")    # the default
measure(g, convention = "networkx")
measure(g, convention = "sna")
measure(g, convention = "ucinet")
```

`convention` is available on `net_degree()`, `net_betweenness()`, `net_closeness()`,
`net_harmonic()`, `net_eigen()`, `net_density()`, and
`net_centralization()`. Other measures have a single convention, stated in
their help pages along with the tools it matches.

```{r}
library(knappnet)
```

## The table

n is the number of nodes, r the number of other nodes a node reaches, and
S the sum of its shortest-path lengths to them.

| | [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/) (default) | [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/) | [sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna) | [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ties | every edge | every edge | adjacency matrix: parallel edges collapse, diagonal ignored | as sna |
| Parallel edges on shortest paths | distinct paths | one path (the shortest edge) | one path | one path |
| Normalized degree | d / (n - 1) | d / (n - 1) | none | d / (n - 1) |
| Normalized betweenness | by pairs not involving the node | same | none | same, as a percentage |
| Closeness | 1 / S, or r / S normalized; only reachable nodes count; `NaN` if r = 0 | (r / S)(r / (n - 1)); distances to the node | (n - 1) / S; 0 if any node is unreachable | (n - 1) / S, unreachable distances set to the longest plus 1 |
| Closeness direction (default) | out | in | out | out (UCINET also reports in) |
| Harmonic centrality | optionally divided by n - 1 | never normalized; distances to the node | divided by n - 1 | divided by n - 1 |
| Eigenvector scale | largest score 1 | unit Euclidean norm | unit norm | unit norm |
| Eigenvector direction | in-ties | in-ties | out-ties | symmetrized |
| Eigenvector, disconnected | computed | refused | computed | a different measure (not implemented; stops) |
| Centralization maxima | allow self-loops by default | (no centralization) | own maxima | own maxima |

The sources are each tool's documentation and, for igraph, NetworkX, and
sna, their behavior when run: the validation suite compares every
convention with the tool itself. UCINET's conventions are those of version
6.849, taken from its help pages and from the port of its routines by its
authors (Borgatti, Agneessens, and Everett 2026); UCINET is not yet run by
the validation suite.

The rest of this article shows each row on a small network.

## Ties: edges or an adjacency matrix

[sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna) and [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home) store a network as an adjacency matrix. Two recorded ties
between the same people become one cell, and a self-loop is a diagonal
cell they ignore. [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/) and [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/) count every edge:

```{r}
multi <- net_frame(data.frame(source = c("a", "a", "b", "c"),
                             target   = c("b", "b", "c", "c")), directed = FALSE)
multi$edges
data.frame(node   = multi$nodes$name,
           igraph = net_degree(multi),
           sna    = net_degree(multi, convention = "sna"))
```

Under igraph's convention, `a` has two edges to `b`, and `c`'s self-loop
adds 2 (both of its ends are at `c`). `loops = FALSE` drops loops but keeps
parallel edges.

## Parallel edges on shortest paths

Here `a` and `b` are joined twice, and there are two routes between `a`
and `c`, through `b` or through `d`:

```{r}
paths <- net_frame(data.frame(source = c("a", "a", "b", "a", "d"),
                             target   = c("b", "b", "c", "d", "c")), directed = FALSE)
data.frame(node     = paths$nodes$name,
           igraph   = round(net_betweenness(paths), 3),
           networkx = round(net_betweenness(paths, convention = "networkx"), 3),
           sna      = round(net_betweenness(paths, convention = "sna"), 3))
```

[igraph](https://r.igraph.org/) counts each parallel edge as a separate shortest path, so of the
three shortest paths from `a` to `c`, two pass through `b`. [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/), [sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna),
and [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home) see one tie between `a` and `b`, so the two routes count
equally. With weights, NetworkX keeps the shortest of the parallel edges;
sna and UCINET do not use weights for betweenness.

## Normalization

Normalized scores divide by the largest value possible in a network of
the same size. [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/), [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/), and [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home) agree on the divisors for
degree and betweenness; UCINET reports some of them as percentages, which
knappnet never does, so multiply by 100 to compare. [sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna) has no
normalization for these measures (its `rescale` divides by the sum
instead).

```{r}
g <- net_frame(data.frame(source = c("a", "a", "a", "b"), target = c("b", "c", "d", "c")),
              directed = FALSE)
data.frame(node             = g$nodes$name,
           betweenness      = net_betweenness(g),
           normalized       = round(net_betweenness(g, normalized = TRUE), 3),
           ucinet_percent   = round(100 * net_betweenness(g, normalized = TRUE,
                                                      convention = "ucinet"), 1),
           sna_rescale      = round(net_betweenness(g) / sum(net_betweenness(g)), 3))
```

## Closeness when some nodes cannot be reached

Closeness is the classic disagreement. In this network `a`, `b`, and `c`
form a path, and `d` and `e` are a separate pair:

```{r}
split <- net_frame(data.frame(source = c("a", "b", "d"), target = c("b", "c", "e")),
                  directed = FALSE)
data.frame(
  node     = split$nodes$name,
  igraph   = round(net_closeness(split), 3),
  networkx = round(net_closeness(split, convention = "networkx"), 3),
  sna      = net_closeness(split, convention = "sna"),
  ucinet   = round(net_closeness(split, convention = "ucinet"), 3)
)
```

- **[igraph](https://r.igraph.org/)** counts only the nodes each node can reach, so `d` and `e`,
  one step from everyone they can reach, look perfectly central.
- **[NetworkX](https://networkx.org/)** multiplies by the share of the network reached, r / (n - 1)
  (Wasserman and Faust 1994, p. 201), which pulls `d` and `e` down.
- **[sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna)** gives 0 to any node that cannot reach every other, which here is
  everyone.
- **[UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home)** replaces each missing distance with one more than the longest
  observed distance, by default.

None is wrong; they answer slightly different questions. Harmonic
centrality, the sum of 1 / distance, sidesteps the problem because an
unreachable node simply adds 0, and the tools agree on it up to
normalization and direction:

```{r}
data.frame(node       = split$nodes$name,
           igraph     = net_harmonic(split),
           networkx   = net_harmonic(split, convention = "networkx"),
           sna_ucinet = net_harmonic(split, convention = "sna"))
```

In directed networks NetworkX measures distances *to* each node and the
others distances *from* it; `mode` overrides the convention's choice.

## Eigenvector centrality: scale and direction

[igraph](https://r.igraph.org/) scales scores so the largest is 1; [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/), [sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna), and [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home) scale
them to unit length. In directed networks, igraph (with `directed = TRUE`)
and NetworkX score a node by who points to it, sna by whom it points to,
and UCINET symmetrizes the network first:

```{r}
d <- net_frame(data.frame(source = c("a", "b", "c", "b", "c"),
                         target   = c("b", "c", "a", "a", "b")))
data.frame(node     = d$nodes$name,
           igraph   = round(net_eigen(d), 3),
           networkx = round(net_eigen(d, convention = "networkx"), 3),
           sna      = round(net_eigen(d, convention = "sna"), 3),
           ucinet   = round(net_eigen(d, convention = "ucinet"), 3))
```

igraph's R function ignores direction unless `directed = TRUE` is given;
`mode = "all"` reproduces that.

On a disconnected network the leading eigenvector is not unique. igraph and
sna still return one (knappnet warns), NetworkX refuses, and UCINET
reports a different measure computed within components; the `"networkx"`
convention refuses too, and `"ucinet"` stops rather than return something
UCINET would not:

```{r, error = TRUE}
net_eigen(split, convention = "networkx")
```

## Centralization

Freeman centralization divides the spread of scores by the largest spread
possible in a network of the same size, which a star attains. For degree,
[igraph](https://r.igraph.org/)'s theoretical maximum by default allows for self-loops, so even a
perfect star without loops scores below 1; [sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna)'s and [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home)'s do not:

```{r}
star <- net_frame(data.frame(source = "hub", target = c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e")),
                 directed = FALSE)
c(igraph          = net_centralization(star, "degree"),
  igraph_no_loops = net_centralization(star, "degree", loops = FALSE),
  sna             = net_centralization(star, "degree", convention = "sna"),
  ucinet          = net_centralization(star, "degree", convention = "ucinet"))
```

`?centralization` lists every maximum. [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/) has no centralization
index, so `convention = "networkx"` is an error there.

## Density

With every edge counted, parallel edges and loops can push density above
1, as in [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/) and [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/). [sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna) and [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home) count each pair once:

```{r}
c(igraph = net_density(multi), sna = net_density(multi, convention = "sna"))
```

## Measures with one convention

Measures where tools agree, or where knappnet follows one tool and the
others are not comparable, take no `convention` argument. Their help pages
state every choice: for example, `net_coreness()` counts parallel edges and
loops as [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/) does ([NetworkX](https://networkx.org/) refuses multigraphs), `net_constraint()` ignores
self-loops (NetworkX counts them), and `net_triad_census()` counts parallel
edges once (igraph's census does not support them). The validation
manifest records each of these differences with its reason; see
[validation](validation.html).
